utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Defence has filed a motion for adjournment in which it asks an adjournment for six months, which would mean that, inclusive the summer recess, would restart late August. The second part of the motion, or at least the second request, is to have oral argument on the matter. That part is granted now, so, Mr. Stewart, you have the opportunity to address the Chamber in relation to that motion. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: May I stay straight away that you're largely going to have the pleasure of hearing from Ms. Loukas on this particular application today. I just need to mention, if I may, a couple of points, one relatively minor, at least I hope so, one perhaps not quite so trivial. The first point, Your Honour, is, simply, that in paragraph 15 of our motion, we had said that, apart from Ms. Cmeric, the only previous member of the Defence team who had been a B/C/S speaker was Mr. Jovanovic, but it occurred to us later that we did have a part-time young man working for us, Mr. Drazen Djukic. At one point he worked for us for something like 40 days, or something over all, and he was a B/C/S speaker. We wanted to get that on the record for accuracy. We don't suggest that -- he made a significant difference at the time, but overall now it doesn't. Your Honour, the second point is slightly less relatively incidental, which is that Your Honours will have noticed that Ms. Cmeric is not in court, and Ms. Loukas mentioned earlier that Ms. Cmeric was about to leave the Defence team, and it is expected that she will finally leave us next Monday. I regret this and will be sorry to lose Ms. Cmeric with whom I have very much enjoyed working. The important point is this, Your Honour, that neither Mr. Krajisnik nor I, as his lead counsel, are in a position to prevent Ms. Cmeric from leaving. She's not in the same position as counsel. She doesn't have to apply to the Registrar for permission to leave the case. I should stress she has given me very fair notice and warning. She's dealt with it, as I would have always have expected from her, entirely professionally and fairly. So there is no issue whatever there. But it is her decision to leave. And Mr. Krajisnik cannot prevent her, and neither can I on his behalf. It has this significance, Your Honour: That, of course, any changeover of case manager is inevitably going to be disruptive, and that is an element. It is not at the very heart of this application for a long adjournment, but it is nevertheless going to be in the immediate future a real difficulty for us. Your Honour, I have not yet been able to make arrangements to replace Ms. Cmeric. We thought we had managed to achieve such arrangements in the last few days, but we haven't. That is going to be difficult. But, Your Honour, as far as paragraph 17 of the motion is concerned, where we say there have been and are problems over Mr. Krajisnik's assessed contribution to his defence costs, but we say those problems have not aggravated to any appreciable degree the difficulties to the Defence team in The Hague in getting on top of this case. Your Honour, that has to be of its very nature a professional assertion by us as the Defence team, and it's, of course, qualified by any appreciable degree, because it wouldn't be right and wouldn't be fair to suggest that it has had absolutely no impact at all. But we do tell Your Honours as conscientious as we can that it hasn't affected the matter so far to any appreciable degree. But, Your Honour, we do just say that we do recognise, and this is always a difficult thing for the client to understand sometimes, that our duties to Mr. Krajisnik cannot interfere with our overriding duty to be straightforward and honest with the Trial Chamber. And at any point where any such assertion on our part ceases to be correct, or might be misleading towards the Trial Chamber, then we won't shrink from our duty in saying so. And, Your Honour, we must make it clear that what we have said in paragraph 17 means what it says. But, Your Honour, we're not able to say that for, for example, the period during which we are seeking an adjournment, paragraph 17 would remain true. And it is only right that we should discharge our duty to the Trial Chamber by making that clear. I don't believe -- I hope Your Honour won't expect me to go any more into the matter, because to some extent it's the future anyway and I don't know exactly what's going to happen. I don't even know exactly when I'm going to get another case manager. But, Your Honour, I hope we have discharged our duty as far as it goes today in giving Your Honours that particular observation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the Chamber appreciates your submissions in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours, you'll hear no more from me for the moment anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Loukas, I do understand that you want to address the Chamber in relation to the motion for adjournment. I have looked at the clock. Perhaps I should have done that before Mr. Stewart started, but, Ms. Loukas, how much time do you think you would need to add or to summarise, to some extent, the motion?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I can indicate that, of course, the Trial Chamber has allowed 35 minutes, I can indicate that I would come in under that estimate, Your Honour. I would be thinking at around about 25 minutes, including about five minutes of photographs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Depending on how long the photographs take.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: But my aim is to come in at about 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, of course it's difficult for you to forecast how much you'd need, or you, Mr. Tieger, not yet knowing what Ms. Loukas is going to tell us. But would you have any idea on how much time you would need?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, before hearing about the anticipated presentation, including the photographs, I would have estimated approximately 10 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: But I agree with the Court that it's a little difficult to tell before hearing the presentation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that means that we'll be able to finish this oral argument today, which the Chamber intended to do, but the Chamber always first would like to know how much time the parties need. Ms. Loukas, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. I would indicate, of course, at the outset that 25 minutes that I've indicated doesn't include questions from the Bench, which would, of course, alter that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's start, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Your Honours, there is one thing I wish to make clear at the outset, and that, of course, is something that Your Honours are more than aware of, but that is nevertheless important to state in the public interest and for the benefit of the public, and that is, of course, that a Tribunal under the auspices of the United Nations must apply the standards of the United Nations. And, of course, there I'm speaking specifically of the standard of the international covenant on civil and political rights, and that is, of course, critical to the legitimacy of the Tribunal. Now, I don't propose to spend a lot of time on the law, Your Honours. The law is clear under Article 21 of the Tribunal's Statute, and of course that corresponds with Article 14 of the international covenant of civil/political rights in relation to a fair trial. The fundamental point is this: The right of the accused to have adequate time and facilities for the preparation of his defence, that is the crux of the issue today. And the facts in that regard, Your Honours, I would submit are clear, that is, firstly, there is -- it cannot be cavilled with the fact that this is an extremely complex case, an important case, an extremely serious case. And it is a case, Your Honour, that involves a massive volume of material that needs to be read and analysed. And our basic Defence submission, Your Honours, is this: That we, as conscientious, responsible, professionals put before the Trial Chamber the fact that we cannot diligently pursue the Defence of Mr. Krajisnik under the current timetable. The current timetable proposed by the Trial Chamber and recorded in the minutes of the United Nations Security Council meeting of the 18th of January this year make a fair trial impossible for Mr. Krajisnik. Now, the specific detail and the specific implications of that statement, Your Honour, is contained at pages 6 and 7 of the written submissions of the Defence. And, Your Honours, it's clear there that the entire exercise of reading and analysing the relevant material has not been completed, and we are already one year into the trial. The fact is, and it's been clear when one reads the trial transcript, which of course His Honour Judge Hanoteau has, that there's been significant attention to this problem by the Defence. We filed a previous motion in July; we've made a number of statements in court. But when one looks at the exercise of effective preparation of cross-examination, Your Honour, it's quite clear that, other than for crime-based witnesses where there has been effective cross-examination, that has been at the price of sacrificing all other work in the case that needs to be done. And, of course, with witnesses that go beyond the crime base into the critical linkage area, and this is the area, of course, in which the agreed facts process broke down, the fact that we have not had a comprehensive reading and analysis of the relevant and potentially relevant documents means that our cross-examination, in the Prosecution case, is hampered. The other aspect of that, of course, is the inadequately developed defence strategy. Your Honours, again, with the baseline of not having gone through all the relevant material, Your Honours, our defence is undermined. Now, the next critical aspect is the Defence case. We have not identified our Defence experts. We have not had adequate time to interview witnesses as counsel in the former Yugoslavia. And another critical aspect, Your Honours, the taking of proper and adequate instructions from Mr. Krajisnik in relation to preparing an effective defence is hampered by the fact that we, the Defence team, are not across the documents. It's as simple as that. Your Honours, at every point of those particular, specific implications of a fair trial, we are under the minimum standard. Now, Your Honours, lead counsel has asked me to place on the record that he has actively discouraged finer legal research in an attempt to deal with all the competing priorities that we must deal with. Constantly, Your Honours, in our effort to ensure that we're doing everything that we can do to present an effective defence for Mr. Krajisnik, under every one of those headings, we end up in colloquial terms, jack of all trades and master of none. Your Honour, in these circumstances, it might be tempting to use the scapegoat of blaming the Defence, but, of course, Your Honour, that is no answer to a timetable-created or judicially-created or Security Council-created ineffective defence and inadequate time for preparation to blame the Defence. That, Your Honours, would be blaming the victim. Now, Your Honours, the Defence is fully aware of the fact that we are dealing with public funds. The international community has an interest in ensuring fiscal responsibility for the use of these funds. That is a given, and we don't argue with that. But it must never be forgotten that the international community has an overriding and paramount interest in fair trials. And if this trial is not fair, Your Honours, the money is wasted and more money will have to be spent. And, of course, Your Honours, justice is no mere mathematical exercise, but there is an area in which mathematics does become relevant, and that is the simple mathematical exercise of dividing up how much material there is to be read and analysed and the time available to read it. And, of course, in making those calculations, Your Honours, Defence counsel would also need time to sleep and even down time, because, quite frankly, if the Defence team is pushed to such a point where, like any other human being, any other legal professional, where we become burnt out, that is entirely counter-productive for justice. Now, Your Honours, we have asked the Prosecution for their best available information or estimate of the total quantity of hard copy and electronic documentation that has been supplied to the Defence since the case began, and of course His Honour Judge Hanoteau would be aware that, prior to the current counsel coming into the case, it was previously lead counsel who was removed from the case by the Tribunal due to his disbarment in New York. A lot of that material that we received from the previous counsel we did not receive until the end of November 2003, and the trial started early February 2004. We have spent a lot of time attempting to sort and sift through that material. If one looks at, overall, what the Prosecution have put forward, have disclosed, initially it was something like 15.000 documents. One adds to that all the 92 bis witness statements and related transcripts. One adds to that the viva voce witness statements and transcripts. And one adds to that new witnesses that have emerged since the filing of the pre-trial brief. The core collection is something in the nature of 8.000 documents. Your Honours, I want to refer specifically to the annexes, and prior to going to that, Your Honours, it might be an opportunity, just to give Your Honours a visual example of the kind of issues we are dealing with here. This should not take very long, but this is a representation of the material that we have currently in our office January and February of this year. The first series of documents are January 2005, and the next series of photographs are February 2005. That is January 2005, Your Honours, and I can indicate that that's -- and we can move on to the next photo. I can talk through the examination of the photos. That is after a lot of sorting of ill-sorted material that came from the previous counsel in attempting to deal with the duplicates we also had. We can move on to the next photo. That's a rather tidier section that has been sorted. This photo, I think, is taken in February, after a lot more sorting had been achieved in relation to ensuring that we attempted to get rid of duplicates and what have you that existed in the hard copies. Sorry, that last one was January, Your Honours. Mr. Stewart was the photographer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I just know the numbering, Your Honours. The 700s are January and the 900s are February.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And here we are, Your Honours, in February now, finally. So, Your Honours, that's just to give Your Honours a visual interpretation of what we're dealing with, because often it's the case, in oral submissions, or merely the presentation of numbers on our annexes can't give a full picture of what we're attempting to deal with. That is the hard copies. There are, of course, a whole series of CDs and what have you, some of which, of course, are duplicates, but we have not been able to perform that sifting exercise to ensure that we know what we're dealing -- and the most critical aspect of this, of course, is that we asked, prior to the trial commencing, that we could have the entire Prosecution disclosure in electronic searchable format, but the Prosecution, due to their own resource problems, of course, were not able to provide that. And we, of course, in the time available, have not been able to ensure that all this material has gone on Xylab, that particular computer function. But what I want to do is give a specific example here in relation to our annexes, and that is that, if we are to leave aside the material that's contained on the Electronic Disclosure Suite, which, if one comes to some sort of sifting exercise in relation to that material, at one minute a page, assuming we're dealing with four pages per document, it would take ten years to sift through the entire general collection. But I'm leaving the Electronic Disclosure Suite out of these submissions for the moment. The example I want to give is this: Say, for example, we want to come to a low estimate of material that we just want to sift, one minute per page, of 250.000 pages, leaving aside issues of audiotapes, videotapes, and what have you, a sifting exercise of 250.000 pages takes, at one minute a page, is 4.200 hours. Now, I hope my mathematics are correct, Your Honour, because mathematics were not my strong suite at university. But nevertheless, that amounts to something like 60 -- if someone was doing that at 60 hours a week, that would take a person 70 weeks. Now, if you get four people doing that, full time, 60 hours a week, that takes four months. That, Your Honour, is an example of the massive scale of the problem that we are dealing with. I want to make this point clear, Your Honours: This claim of six months is not put forward as some sort of negotiating claim or some sort of ambit claim or something for horse-trading. This is something that we, as responsible, conscientious, legal professionals say that we need to ensure that we can provide an effective Defence. Your Honours are not interested and we are not interested in putting up some sort of superficial show-trial defence. That's not what we want; that's not what you want. Because the ability of the Defence to prepare its case is affected by these problems, but not just that. The ability of the Trial Chamber to try this case fairly and efficiently is ultimately affected by these problems. Your Honours, it's our submission that the Trial Chamber cannot take any unwarranted risks with a fair trial. We make this point, Your Honours: That when experienced counsel are telling the Trial Chamber and the public that we ourselves are not presenting an effective defence, why would we do that unless it were true? And, Your Honours, one needs to look at the fact that I filed a motion for withdrawal last October, giving specifically, in court, my reasons due to inadequacy of time and the consequences that has for a fair trial for Mr. Krajisnik, and Ms. Cmeric's resignation, in those terms. The international community, Your Honours, has entrusted this Tribunal with a task of trying persons charged with serious violations of international humanitarian law, and the international community expects the Tribunal to do so in accordance with the rights of the accused. The fundamental point is that if the Tribunal is not given sufficient time and money to do so by the international community, then the Tribunal should not attempt to try those persons in a way which does not accord with those rights. Of course, it has been said by Judge Hunt in an appeals decision that this Tribunal will not be judged only -- "this Tribunal will not be judged by the number of convictions which it enters or by the speed with which it concludes the completion strategy which the Security Council has endorsed, but by the fairness of its trials." Others have said that this Tribunal will not be judged by the number of convictions or the speed but also by the fairness of its trial. Whatever formulation Your Honours prefer, the fact is that nobody in this courtroom wants the trial against Mr. Krajisnik to be part of that spreading stain. This case will play a central role in shaping the legacy and the jurisprudence of this Tribunal, and without a fair trial, that legacy will be flawed, it will be stained, and it will be a legacy that is not worth having. Your Honours, we, the Defence, do not want that, the Trial Chamber does not want that, and the international community does not want that. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Loukas. Mr. Tieger, may I take it that you will respond? Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour. Thank you very much. Your Honour, it is correct that the central issue is whether adequate time for preparation of the Defence has been provided. It's our submission that that question was answered in September of last year for Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. two reasons: First, in the well-reasoned decision by the Trial Chamber addressing the same issue; and second, because the time sought by the Defence for adequate preparation on their own terms of that defence was, through happenstance, provided. And let me retrace some of the backdrop very quickly in order to explain that. In December 2003 - and these issues are raised in the Court's decision - the Defence sought a trial schedule that would include some 70 extraordinary non-sitting days between February 2nd and August 1st, 2004. As it happened, between February 2nd and mid-July 2004, there were 75 working days during which no court hearings took place. Nevertheless, on July 14th, the Defence made a formal motion for an extended adjournment seeking adjournment until 4 October 2004. Although the specific number of days weren't calculated, by my own calculation which I admit is approximate, that entailed roughly 42 extraordinary days of adjournment in addition to the scheduled summer recess. The Court denied that motion for the reasons stated in its decision of September 21st. Nevertheless, the Defence received the benefit of all the time which it had requested. Since that request, there have been approximately 70 extraordinary working days in which no court hearings took place, in addition to the end-of-the-year or new year break. And of course that calculation includes the time between Judge El Mahdi's announcement and today's proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do not correctly understand if you would like to include the recesses -- you said in addition to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, beyond -- right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now it's clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes. It's also important, I think, to look with -- look again at the issues raised by -- the specific issues raised by the Defence in its motion for some clarity. That motion focused in particular on the voluminous nature of the materials and their searchability, at least as I followed the motion. And as the Court can see on pages 3 and 4, in connection with the nature or the volume of material provided, the Defence outlines and enumerates approximately 200.000 pages of material, 103 video tapes, 351 CDs, 24.800 documents in the Krajisnik case collection, 26.725 files in their hard disk. Well, first of all, it's important to note for clarification that those individual recitations represent essentially the same body of material, and I'll attempt, in just a moment, to describe the history of disclosure to identify where those collections came from. A few other factors may be useful to note. For example, for a variety of reasons, on various occasions, CD disclosures or DVDs disclosures contained one or two documents which were disclosed in that format for searchability. But let me retrace very quickly the rough history of disclosure to indicate both the providence of those documents and their relationship, one to another. As Ms. Loukas indicated earlier, the Prosecution disclosed to the Defence team at the time that -- Mr. Brashich and Mr. Kostich who were charged with the responsibility for that case, in excess of 15.000 documents, approximately 17.500 documents, is my understanding. In addition to that hard-copy disclosure, eight CDs that were Xy-searchable were disclosed. Now, Xy-searchable, although the Court may be familiar with that vehicle, means that it's possible to type in a word and then pull up all the documents that mention that particular word. Those CDs were also made available to the Defence team when they took over for Mr. Brashich and Mr. Kostich. In addition, the Prosecution also provided an index to the hard-copy documents. Now, that index had a description of the particular documents, with such things as the date of the document, the author of the document, the body which sent the document, and so on. So it would be possible to go down the index and identify particular documents of relevance and then relate them back to the CDs that were -- that could be searched. The Prosecution also provided a reduced or focused list of potential exhibits or documents that reflected the most relevant or significant documents in view of the Prosecution, the documents that would be focused on by the Prosecution during the course of its case. And that was provided with an index in 3-Ds so that the index could be electronically searched. In addition, the index was hyperlinked, meaning that if there was a document of interest to anyone viewing it, that that document could be called up with simply the click of a mouse. Now, the Defence raised some concerns about the fact that there were eight CDs and therefore they had to search the CDs individually rather than being able to type in a word and go immediately through all documents. Our support people urged them to put the CDs into their hard drive, and eventually the Prosecution offered to put the CDs into hard drive and did so for the Defence. Those are the materials that are, in fact, in the hard drive, the materials that were previously disclosed on the CDs and were now then placed in the hard drive. Now, the Xy-searchability function was lost when they were put in the hard drive, they're not searchable that way, but the index still existed. In addition, after that point, but actually prior to the July 14 motion, we made a request to have those documents put into the Krajisnik collection in EDS, and EDS is word-searchable. Now, I raise that because -- for two reasons: Number 1, to dispel any impression of a cumulative nature of these documents, where the -- it suggests that collections are added one on top of another rather than the redisclosure, in different formats, in order to enhance retrievability or searchability. And I also raise it because it's important to dispel any impression that the review of these documents is done in the abstract or is done out of a particular context. And it is possible to get the sense that the review of these materials must be done as if the Defence came upon this body of material one day and then had to review everything, without any insight whatsoever into the relative significance, priority, importance, or duplicative nature of any of those documents. We, of course, begin with the fact that the Prosecution provided the Defence with a pre-trial brief with respect to witness statements, with 65 ters, with respect to individual witnesses who were called, hyperlinked exhibit lists, and I think Mr. Treanor and Ms. Hanson are among the best examples of that. All of Mr. Treanor's documents, which provided at the outset of the case, a very significant and, in some respects, nearly comprehensive insight into those documents of greater significance with respect to those issues, were presented in an index and were hyperlinked and were readily accessible. But it's also important to bear in mind that, as the case proceeds, not all the documents that were originally disclosed retain their original potential significance for a variety of reasons. Number 1, many of them have been explained; number 2, witnesses have been dropped; number 3, issues have been refined. For example, although there has been no significant movement between the Prosecution and the Defence toward agreed facts on various issues, it is surely the case that the Defence has made its own formulations and decisions about which issues remain genuinely in controversy and which issues they intend to focus their attention on. It's no longer the case that these documents simply exist without any outlying significance that renders all the search vehicles available as meaningful as they, in fact, are. Your Honour, I'd like to make just a couple of points in response to a few comments made by Ms. Loukas. I'm not aware that the projected trial date is a reflection of the so-called completion strategy or any outlying directives. My recollection is it is quite consistent with the original estimations of this trial, and it's certainly consistent with what, I believe, any objective observer would think as a reasonable period of time within which to conduct such a case. I would remind the Court that delays have a number of potentially pernicious impacts on the administration of justice. Witnesses grow weary, witnesses are lost, case managers are lost, personnel are lost. The Prosecution, too, has suffered as a result of the length of the trial. The reference to a ten-year period of time to review the general collection material, I presume, is somewhat of a throw-away, and I think should be treated as such. The fact that collection of documents from other cases exist in EDS is not particularly relevant to this inquiry, and I don't think should be treated as such, although it leaves a general flavor of volume that I think is potentially misleading and should be addressed. I'm not sure where Ms. Loukas came up with the figure of 250.000 pages, but I understood that they estimated 200.000 pages, B/C/S and English, which I think reduces to a review of 100.000 pages. If the Court wishes to engage in a calculation, I think that's a more fairer place to begin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To clarify the matter, Ms. Loukas, it's just my recollection that 206.000 were mentioned in the motion. You mentioned 250.000.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I was giving it as an example of when one takes into account the various formats that we have to look through, an example of the sifting exercise that would have to be performed to ensure that what's an important document, what's a duplicate, what we need to be concerned with, a comparison of documents between B/C/S and English, and just on the basis of one minute a page. That was the -- it was done as an air exercise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The document you mentioned in the motion was slightly smaller. It was 206.500.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, it was 206.500.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that would include two languages. Because to this moment, I did understand your explanation of what it takes to deal with them. But Mr. Tieger is talking about 200.000, two languages, and so splits that up in two and says 100.000, and you went up from 206.500 to 250.000. That's what you mentioned, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour, because when one looks at the material in the annex, firstly, we do concede, and I conceded for my example, that a lot of what's contained on the hard disk is duplication. We're not entirely sure that it's all duplication because we haven't gone through the sifting exercise. And to ensure that we aren't missing something does require something of a sifting exercise, not just through the material that we've already got in B/C/S and English in hard copy in our office, and of course there's the necessity to go through both English and B/C/S just in terms of confirming translations and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand. The only matter I wanted to clarify at this moment is that Mr. Tieger is talking about 200.000, where I had 206 in my memory, which was 206.500, and we're all talking about the same material.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, those are essentially our submissions. As a minor matter, I would note that the estimate of the core collection, I believe, is a case of adding two disclosures together, the original estimate -- the original disclosure and then the subsequent one, which included the original. So I think it's -- I think Ms. Loukas estimated 8.000, and I think it's closer to 55 or 60 per cent of that total, the first disclosure and the second disclosure. Not a significant point in light of my other comments. But for the reasons mentioned, including the legitimate expectations of both parties and the Court, and the objective time and opportunities provided, the Prosecution opposes this motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. We have ten minutes left. Let me first ask whether the --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, might I make a couple of observations. I absolutely do not do anything other than entirely endorse and support what my co-counsel said. I should make that 100 per cent clear. Put one comment, it was a forensic comment made by Mr. Tieger, but as far as the loss of case managers because cases go slowly, Your Honour, I have refrained, because she has made her own decision. But Ms. Cmeric is not leaving because this case is going too slowly, she's leaving because it's going too fast and she's leaving because there isn't an adequate opportunity to prepare the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, Mr. Stewart, I intended to give a brief opportunity to respond, but first wanted to see if the Judges had any questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: My apologies, Your Honour. I didn't wish to be importunate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would, just for clarification matters, I would have two questions. The first is to the Defence: The Hague team, what do you exactly understand by The Hague team? We do understand more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, indeed Your Honour -- should I say straight away, Your Honour, Ms. Loukas and I, through my left ear, are very amicably agreed that I should deal with this question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The Hague team, as it's constituted at the moment, is myself at lead counsel, Ms. Loukas as co-counsel, Ms. Cmeric for another week as case manager, and let us assume, notionally, that it will continue to consist of a case manager when we find a suitable person to take on that job. It consists additionally of Ms. Kelly Pitcher, who is a full-time legal assistant with us, and will be with us for a few more months. It consists of Ms. Catriona Vine, who is only with us until Easter -- has been with us for a short time which, obviously, despite her undoubted skills and experience, she's an English barrister so that goes without saying, of course. But despite her skills and experience, that's a short time. The case of course does limit the contribution that anybody can humanly make. And we have a part-time intern, a very bright young man, Mr. Kevin Afghani, but he's only with us for two days a week because he's a full-time student. We do have Mr. Jovanovic in London, doing his course at the London School of Economics. So he's, sort of, part of The Hague team. And we have very -- again, with no disparagement at all, we have very minor assistance, because of the time they're able to give, from interns. So the permanent Hague team -- we hoped it would be permanent -- but in Ms. Cmeric's case it isn't quite. But I call usually -- we refer to as the core team has been myself, Ms. Loukas, and Ms. Cmeric, and we do have Ms. Pitcher at the moment as well as a legal assistant. We have consistently had at least one and, for quite a long time, for several months, we had two full-time legal assistants. We have Ms. Dixon, whom Your Honours may remember, and Mr. Jovanovic for a period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us approximately, these legal assistants, for how long you had them?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, Ms. Dixon -- from memory, Ms. Dixon, I think, was with us for about four or five months. I know the material is in here, Your Honour, but it's going to be quicker, Your Honour, if I give you a reasonable estimate. But the position was, Your Honour, we did have, from the beginning -- very early in the trial right through to now, we have always had at least one full-time legal assistant, and for a period of about four months or five months, I think it was, over the summer until he had to go to London to start his degree course, we have Mr. Jovanovic as well, so there was a period when we had two. There was also a short overlap period between Ms. Dixon, as she was on the way out, and Ms. Pitcher as she was on the way in, but that is just while they hand over and get used to each other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This leads me to my next question: The remuneration of The Hague team, does Mr. Krajisnik in any way contribute to that, in financial terms?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, he doesn't, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He doesn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: He doesn't. Perhaps, Your Honour, I can say, because it is an important topic and I do understand that, and we mentioned it in the motion, perhaps I can say this: First of all, Your Honour, the whole question is a bone of contention between Mr. Krajisnik and me. That has, I think, been pretty obvious. I won't go any more into that, but it is, unfortunately. What happens is that I, as lead counsel, allocate the funds coming from the Registry to fund The Hague team. That is what I have done since the beginning of the trial. What I don't do is allocate funds anywhere else. So The Hague team, I'm not suggesting it's luxury, Your Honour, but The Hague team, we have been able to sustain at that size. And although, more money, of course, Your Honour, can always give rise to more resources, but as I think, perhaps, I've commented in the past, the one thing that the projected budget and the allowed budget would never have allowed us to do, for example, is to have three counsel, which is a matter which would always have made a great difference, of course, Your Honour, if we ever had that. But that would have been, however one allocated the judgement, that would have always been impossible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber is aware of the budget. We just wanted to know the composition of the team in relation to remuneration. Thank you for that answer, Mr. Stewart. I think I've got no further questions at this moment for the parties. Would you like to respond to what Mr. Tieger said?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. First of all, I do find in relation to Mr. Tieger's run-through, which is helpful in the sense that it makes it clear what the Prosecution is saying, but Mr. Tieger's run-through of, well, they provided this and they provided that and these files were there, is a little difficult for me, Your Honour, because that's something which I would like the opportunity to go through with Ms. Cmeric. Because one thing struck me immediately. For example, When Mr. Tieger described the Prosecution as urging the Defence to put the CDs on its hard disk and then described as if we were babies - I don't mean he meant it offensively - but if we were babies that didn't know how to do that. The Prosecution came along and helped us to put the CDs on the hard disk. Your Honour, that's not the way it is. My case manager knows how to put CDs on a hard disk. I know how to put CDs on a hard disk. After all, I provided the file of scanned photographs -- digital photographs that I handed over today. We do know how to do those things. As far as I recall, what didn't happen, although I wasn't involved with the nuts and bolt of Mr. Carolyn [phoen] and Ms. Cmeric sitting down to do it, because that's not a valuable use of lead counsel's time. It wasn't the CDs. They didn't come over and show us like babies how to install our own CDs, they brought, as far as I recall, their own set of CDs which was in an organised state which we were having serious problems with, and it was that that was installed on our hard disk. So that one point about which I do have one piece of familiarity indicates to me that the description -- I hope I'm right about that, Your Honour, because I'm just recalling what I do know. But that leads me, like a clock striking 13, to wonder about the other things with which I'm not technically familiar, because I don't do these things if I can avoid it because I have a case manager to do that, Your Honour. First of all, I really would like the opportunity of going through that with my case manager to be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't think it's one of the main issues. I don't believe that Mr. Tieger wanted to depict you as babies, at least as electronic babies. At the same time, it's clear that if you say -- if you come up with newly organised material and you put it on our computer, then of course that's not the same as putting on a computer all the diskette material. It's not the core of the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's an illustration of it, if I may say, Your Honour, because it's this: The picture which comes across -- what I can say without entering into the technicalities, the picture that comes across of some source of organised, easy-to-manage, categorised material is a picture which I simply don't recognise. I don't recognise it in relation to the CDs. I didn't get eight CDs from Mr. Brashich, I got 50 CDs all over the shop with thousands of files on them. It doesn't match at all the absolute -- and not just the literal picture that one sees on the screen, but the actual knowledge I have of what is actually down there at our office, at the Dutch bar. Because within every one of those files, practically, is something that still needs organising. For example, Your Honour, of the days available in this recent break, since Judge El Mahdi retired, I have done an analysis of how we have spent our time, and in my case, Your Honour, I have spent something like 50 per cent of what you might call the discretionary time, if you take away the unvoidable tasks, the things that have got to be done - the 92 bis responses, the motions, helping draft this motion, for example, all the things which actually had to be done, motions for protective measures, things like that, that had to be done according to deadlines, time tables, had to be split between us - once you take away all those tasks and then you go down to the discretionary tasks in the sense of having some management ability to decide what do you do this/that day, what task do you give priority to, as opposed to having the priority set for you, I have spent something like 50 per cent of my time organising papers. And what exactly I've been doing is, in a sense, not to the point, although it would bear examination, but the essential ingredient of this, Your Honour, is what I've been doing is stuff which I should have been able either to do myself or have somebody else do on my behalf before the trial even started. So here I am in -- and I came back for a couple of days between Christmas and the new year and spent a couple of days just physically going through stuff down at the -- at our office in the Dutch bar, and I was doing things which should have been done, in any ordinary case, could, should, and would have been done, months and weeks before this trial even started, and we are still doing them. And those hundreds of files that one sees down at our office are not organised files. They're organised in the sense they're on the shelves. But when you get into them, they are not organised. We have done the first generation of organisation of that. And then there are tens and tens and tens and tens of thousands of pages of documents. And I haven't read many of them, I don't even know what they are, I don't have enough B/C/S resources to find out what they are. I open a CD and I find thousands of files without any real way of picking my way through them. It is absolutely impossible. And that's why one loses a case manager, because the position is hopeless.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Stewart, was this your response? I'm also looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have one more -- it is an unusual request or suggestion. Your Honour, a lot of information flows around this building --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I first have to ask the interpreters and the technicians whether they could ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand, since I hear no opposition from the technicians and interpreters, but there are also outside services beyond the control of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I shan't be very long, Your Honour, at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: A lot of information flows around this building. It does sometimes make us uncomfortable. We hope we're not paranoid, but just because you're not paranoid doesn't mean people aren't out to get you. But, Your Honour, we are uncomfortable about -- I should say, and I'll say it very briefly in open court, I have personally been subjected to the most scurrilous attack by a former member of my team, with untruthful allegations about how I spend my time when there's an adjournment, how much work I do other than this case, of which I do practically none, Your Honour. And we are so sensitive about this, and we are so anxious about the picture that sometimes seems to get created, that what I would like to do, Your Honour, is I would like to hand up, confidentially, to the Trial Chamber and, of course, to the Prosecution - we have no possible objection to their seeing it - I would like to hand up schedules which I have prepared just showing where Ms. Loukas and I, who are the only two counsel in the case, have been since Judge El Mahdi retired, how long we've been here, and giving some indication of how our -- we're not asking for special consideration from the Trial Chamber as to our personal lives, and we don't wish to go into that, Your Honour, certainly not publicly. But we are asking for it to be recognised and seen in black and white how far we are at the limits of what we can fairly be asked to contribute by way of professional work on this case, and have it seen in black and white how our lives actually work and what we have actually done, in case there is any information floating around this building - and we do pick it up, Your Honour - any information which suggests to the contrary. At the very worst, these pieces of paper are harmless. Your Honours can look at them and say, Well, so what? And that's the worst that can happen. So since that's the worst that could happen, we would like Your Honours to have these pieces of paper, and we would like Your Honours just to see how it works.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, we have considered whether or not we'll accept that. The Chamber comes to the conclusion that there's no need. The rumours you are talking about are not rumours that reached the Trial Chamber to the extent that we got information on what you did, neither have we ever heard of any former team member. On the other hand, if you'd like to prove what the Chamber is willing to accept, that you're hard-working and spending time on the case, then we will not keep you from doing it. But as you said already yourself, the worst that can happen is that we say, So what? I mean, you took that risk. There's no need for us to receive it. But if you'd prefer to do it, we'll not stop you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We would prefer it, Your Honour. What's absolutely the worse that can happen? May I pick out one point from it which Your Honours will see, which is not -- there are aspects of it which Your Honours will see. You'll see why it's confidential, apart from the fact that it mentions, just in passing, it mentions a category which courts are always very careful, which is people are not even legally adult. So that's -- all courts are very careful in relation to those people, and we ask that as well. But, Your Honour, one simple example. I was in court all day on Monday, the 21st, if it was, of December. I went to London for two or three days and I was in court all day. That was the first day in 2004 that I was in court in England. It was the first and only day. And it also -- this schedule also gives just the very barest indication of the tiny degree to which I, and certainly not Ms. Loukas, who gave up a full-time job in Sydney, have been involved in anything else at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So I would like to hand it up, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You provide it to us. Mr. Tieger, there's not much time left, because of the other interests in having this hearing finished. It's about transportation, as you'll understand. Is there anything you'd like to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Unless the Court has any questions, there is no need.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Very well. We will conclude this hearing. The Chamber will consider the matter. The Chamber will receive ... [Trial Chamber and registrar confer].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I understand that you'd like to address the Court. You should be aware that, for transportation reasons, we have to finish very quickly. So if you would like to address the Court, I don't know whether you discussed with Mr. Stewart what you'd like to say, but it's always wise not to surprise your own counsel. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I will not surprise my counsel. I have the following to ask of you, Your Honours: I have submitted a request to the Trial Chamber, because I am concerned about my defence, and I would kindly ask you to set aside a period of time for me to address Your Honours. At one point we did hold these Status Conferences, but there haven't been any recently, and I just wish to raise the need for such a Status Conference to be held. And I would also like to welcome the new Judge and thank him for his kind words. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, you're raising an issue which is not without complexity, Mr. Krajisnik, because if you want to raise anything from the recent past, you may know that the normal way of doing it, and the appropriate way of doing it, is through counsel. I don't know whether, meanwhile, you discussed the matters you'd like to raise with counsel.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to say that whatever both my counsel stated here today, I endorse. I do not have anything to comment -- to raise in relation to the services provided by my counsel. They are very good lawyers. But what I have to say will be helpful both to you and my counsel, because we seem to have this problem, both my counsel and I, that we are unable to solve between the two of us. And that's why I need to raise this matter to Your Honours. And this is a very complex matter where I would need the assistance of this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Krajisnik, you have sent us a letter. This letter has been sent back to you. The Chamber has not kept any copies of this letter. Of course, I can't say that I have forgotten completely about the content, because that's almost impossible. Is that the kind of issue you'd like to raise?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, mostly so. But, in particular, the matter that you mentioned today as regards my contribution to the fees for my defence, and I would like to include that matter as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. From my recollection, that is a matter that was also, to some extent at least, raised in the letter. Have you informed Mr. Stewart about the content of the letter? Has he received a copy of it? We don't have it anymore.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stewart is more or less kept abreast of that. He is faced with these problems, just as I am. Nothing of what I have to say is against my counsel, and I hope, and I believe, that my counsel is aware of the contents of the letter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My question was quite simple, whether he received a copy of it or not, whether you sent him a copy, so that he is fully aware of what was on your mind when you wrote the letter. Wouldn't it have been wisest that you give him a copy of the letter, discuss it with them, then see what remains, and then find a way to address the Chamber at a Status Conference, or at least some time reserved for that aim? I mean, he'll hear anyhow, if you address the Chamber, what you want to say, so therefore ...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, these matters have been topical throughout the period. I did show the letter to my counsel, and it was then forwarded to the Registrar. But if this is not the case, if he hasn't seen the letter, I will certainly make sure that he does.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: If I can simply help factually, Your Honour. Mr. Krajisnik did very fairly indicate to me the main points in his letter, in summary, but I haven't had the letter. And if Mr. Krajisnik has offered to give me a copy of the letter, it would be gratefully received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's do the following: Mr. Krajisnik, the Chamber will consider the matter. But since you have offered to give Mr. Stewart the letter, he might give you some advice or address the matter soon. So at this moment, we will not take a decision on it, but soon we will deal with the matter, if it has been brought to the attention of the Chamber in the appropriate and the usual way. We really have to stop now, because otherwise we are in trouble with your transportation. We, meanwhile, received "Days in The Hague." Mr. Stewart, that's almost a title of a novel.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: There's two novels, Your Honours, one for me and one for Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, two novels. The Chamber will consider the motion. It will take a decision, most likely will give an oral decision relatively soon. That could be tomorrow or the day after tomorrow. But, as we did with the July motion, there certainly will be a reasoning in writing because the matter is too important and it would not be appropriate to deal with it just in a short, oral decision. We'll also consider the matter raised by Mr. Krajisnik once the Defence has further been able to review that matter. For the time being, we'll continue tomorrow. Tomorrow, I take it, Mr. Harmon, the OTP will call its next expert witness, Ms. Hanson.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll adjourn until tomorrow morning, 9.00, courtroom II.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 1st day of March, 2005, at 9.00 a.m.
